claims.summary: Chinese accounts of Funan repeatedly describe coercive capture and enslavement of people from neighboring communities. K'ang T'ai's third-century report, preserved through later Chinese textual traditions, states that inhabitants of towns refusing homage could be abducted and made slaves; later dynastic material repeats coercive enslavement in descriptions of Funan. Specialist archaeological source criticism treats these texts as important but exogenous evidence whose political-geographic claims cannot simply be read as a precise territorial map. The atlas therefore records recurrent enslavement at P2 while preserving the dependence and geographic uncertainty of the textual tradition.

claims.summary: Indigenous Hawaiian historical traditions and later specialist scholarship describe kauwā as a small, hereditary and strongly segregated status group within late precontact Hawaiian society. sources.title: Slavery in First Millennium Arabia: Epigraphy and the Qurʾān

claims.summary: A specialist synthesis of the Ancient South Arabian epigraphic corpus supports the existence of slavery and captive enslavement across first-millennium South Arabia. The evidence includes people contrasted with free persons, explicit proprietorial rights, purchase and sale of enslaved women, hereditary claims over women and descendants, and repeated war-captive deportations. The same scholarship cautions that the common term ʿbd is context-dependent and can also denote attendants or dependants, so this claim does not classify every ʿbd as enslaved or characterize South Arabia as a slave society.

claims.summary: Specialist legal-historical scholarship establishes slavery as a legally defined institution in Sasanian Iran. Enslaved people could be treated as property, inherited with estates, attached to agricultural land, and employed by Zoroastrian fire foundations. Sources of enslavement included captivity, descent, debt bondage and, under restricted conditions, sale of family members. This supports an institutional P3 classification without assuming that enslaved people formed a dominant share of the population or that practice was spatially uniform across the empire.

claims.summary: Specialist archaeological research at fifteenth-century Songo Mnara explicitly investigates the likely presence and material lives of enslaved labourers within the Swahili stone town.
